strengths: Novel and technically sound extension of twisted SMC with locally optimal proposals (inspired by continuous diffusion SMC works) to discrete diffusion models, addressing the non-differentiability of discrete variables via a first-order Taylor approximation combined with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation.

Careful handling of the 'Carry-Over Unmasking' discontinuity in masked diffusion models via a continuous reformulation of the denoising model, with a detailed gradient analysis in the appendix justifying the design choice.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper derives a continuous-time (CTMC) formulation of the SMC importance weights and shows it recovers results from prior discrete-diffusion SMC work (Lee et al., 2025), lending credibility to the framework.

Thoughtful ablations comparing the naive reverse-process proposal, the (intractable) locally optimal proposal (used as oracle), and the proposed first-order approximation, with reward/EMD/diversity/ESS trace analyses that clearly illustrate the trade-offs (e.g., weight degeneracy and diversity loss with naive proposals).

Recognizes and addresses a specific failure mode of masked diffusion (irreversible unmasking) by additionally validating the method on ReMDM and UDLM variants that allow remasking/full mutability, strengthening the practical story.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to toy/small-scale settings: a 2D discretized mixture of Gaussians (64x64 states) and binarized MNIST. None of the motivating real-world applications mentioned in the introduction (molecular generation, materials discovery, math reasoning, language tasks) are evaluated, leaving the practical significance and scalability of the method largely unverified.

No comparison against existing alignment baselines from the literature (e.g., RL-based fine-tuning such as SEPO/GLID2E, other discrete guidance methods like D-CFG/D-CBG, Nisonoff et al. 2024, or Lee et al. 2025's SMC variant). The only baseline is an internally-derived 'approximate guidance' ablation, making it hard to judge how the method compares to the state of the art.

No experiments with large vocabulary sizes or long sequences (e.g., text), despite discrete diffusion language models being a primary motivating application; it's unclear whether the Taylor approximation and Gumbel-Softmax relaxation remain effective/stable at that scale.

Lack of standard quantitative evaluation metrics (e.g., FID or classifier accuracy at scale for images, downstream task metrics for larger tasks) beyond reward, EMD, and simple diversity counts on very small datasets.

No analysis of computational overhead/wall-clock cost of the SMC procedure (multiple particles, resampling, gradient computation via autodiff through Gumbel-Softmax) relative to baselines, which is important for a method marketed as practical for test-time alignment.

The core technical idea (twisted SMC with locally-optimal proposal via first-order Taylor expansion, plus Gumbel-Softmax for discrete gradients) is largely an adaptation of established techniques from continuous diffusion SMC and discrete gradient estimation literature, somewhat limiting novelty.

Authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations section that effectiveness on more complex tasks and broader baseline comparisons remain future work, indicating the current evaluation is preliminary.

strengths: The core technical derivation is sound: the twisted SMC framework with a locally-optimal proposal, its first-order Taylor approximation, and the Gumbel-Softmax/continuous relaxation trick to handle non-differentiability of discrete states and the carry-over-unmasking constraint are all clearly motivated and mathematically well worked out.

Useful theoretical contribution connecting the proposed discrete-time SMC importance weights to continuous-time CTMC-based SMC formulations in the appendix, unifying with prior work (Ou et al., Holderrieth et al., Lee et al.).

The ablation comparing locally-optimal proposal, reverse-process proposal, first-order approximation, and approximate guidance (via reward/EMD/diversity metrics and ESS/resampling traces) is informative and helps build intuition about why the proposed method works better than naive guidance.
Extension to ReMDM and UDLM to address the irreversibility problem of masked diffusion models is a thoughtful practical addition that strengthens the applicability discussion.
Method is training-free and asymptotically unbiased (inherits SMC consistency), which is an attractive practical property relative to fine-tuning-based alignment approaches.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very limited in scale and realism: only a 2D discretized mixture-of-Gaussians toy problem and small binarized (28x28, 2-valued) MNIST are used, despite the introduction motivating the work with molecular generation, materials discovery, and math reasoning — none of which are tested.

No experiments on language/text data, which is arguably the most important application domain for discrete diffusion models given recent interest in diffusion LLMs; the lack of any such experiment substantially limits the demonstrated significance of the contribution.

No empirical comparison against existing published baselines (e.g., Lee et al. 2025 SMC-based debiasing guidance, D-CBG/D-CFG guidance of Schiff et al., Nisonoff et al. guidance, RL fine-tuning baselines) — the paper only compares against internal ablations of its own proposal variants and a simple 'approximate guidance' baseline the authors constructed themselves.

The reported 'oracle' locally-optimal proposal relies on brute-force evaluation over the full state space, which is only tractable for the toy 2D dataset; this highlights that the strongest baseline is not scalable, and the gap in performance/robustness of the practical first-order method versus true SMC guarantees on more complex/high-dimensional tasks is not empirically characterized.

No computational cost/runtime analysis is provided despite the method requiring multiple gradient/backward passes through the denoiser and reward model per step for many particles, which is an important practical consideration for a training-free but potentially expensive test-time method.
No error bars, repeated trials, or statistical significance reporting for the reward/EMD/diversity metrics shown in Figure 1, making it hard to assess robustness of the comparisons.

The paper itself acknowledges in the Limitations section that it has not been evaluated on more complex tasks or benchmarked against a broader set of methods, which is an unusually direct admission that the evaluation section is incomplete for a venue at this level.

The tempering schedule for masked diffusion is described as requiring careful hand-tuning to work at all (Fig. 6, Sec 4.2 discussion), suggesting fragility/sensitivity to hyperparameters that is not systematically studied.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical contribution: extends twisted SMC with locally-optimal proposals to discrete diffusion models, addressing the intractability of exact locally-optimal proposals via a first-order Taylor approximation combined with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation for differentiability in discrete space.

Careful treatment of a subtle but important technical issue: the discontinuity induced by the Carry-Over Unmasking constraint in masked diffusion models, with a principled continuous relaxation (Eq. 16) and a detailed gradient analysis in the appendix justifying the design choice.

Rich theoretical appendix connecting the proposed discrete-time SMC formulation to continuous-time (CTMC) SMC samplers, recovering results consistent with recent concurrent work (Lee et al., 2025), which strengthens the technical grounding of the method.

Good internal ablations comparing the locally-optimal proposal, its first-order approximation, the naive reverse-process proposal, and approximate guidance, with reward/EMD/diversity metrics and ESS/resampling traces that clearly illustrate the trade-offs (weight degeneracy, diversity collapse) motivating the proposed proposal design.

Extends the method beyond masked diffusion to ReMDM and UDLM, showing the approach generalizes and that remasking-based models alleviate the tempering-schedule sensitivity issue observed with standard masked diffusion.
Training-free and (asymptotically) unbiased sampling procedure, which is an appealing property relative to fine-tuning-based alignment methods that risk reward over-optimization.
weaknesses: Experimental evaluation is limited to very small-scale, low-stakes settings: a 2D discretized mixture-of-Gaussians toy task and binarized MNIST. Despite the introduction motivating the work with molecular generation, materials discovery, and math reasoning, no experiments are conducted on any realistic discrete-diffusion application domain (e.g., text/language generation, DNA/protein design, graphs), leaving the practical significance and scalability of the method largely unvalidated.

No comparison against existing published alignment/guidance/fine-tuning baselines discussed at length in the related work (e.g., D-CFG/D-CBG of Schiff et al., Nisonoff et al. guidance, SEPO, GLID2E, Wang et al. 2024 backprop fine-tuning, or the SMC method of Lee et al. 2025). The only baselines are internal ablations of the proposed framework (reverse-process proposal, approximate guidance), which weakens the claim of the method's competitiveness relative to the broader alignment literature.

Quantitative evaluation on MNIST is qualitative/limited (single example reward values and visual inspection); no standard generative-quality metrics (e.g., FID, classifier accuracy over larger sample sets, precision/recall) are reported to substantiate sample fidelity and diversity claims at scale.

Scalability of the core method is questionable: the exact locally-optimal proposal requires O(V^L) reward evaluations, and even the first-order approximation requires differentiating through the reward and denoiser at every SMC step for every particle, which could be costly for large vocabularies/sequence lengths typical of language or protein models; no wall-clock/computation cost comparison against baselines is provided.

The tempering schedule λt is hand-crafted and task-specific; the paper itself acknowledges (Sec. 4.2, Appendix G) that substantial manual tuning was needed to get good results with masked diffusion models, which raises concerns about practical usability and reproducibility across new tasks without similarly careful tuning.

The self-declared limitations (no evaluation on complex tasks, no broader RL/guidance benchmarking, hand-crafted schedules) directly correspond to core weaknesses expected to be addressed for a top-tier venue, suggesting the work is more of a promising proof-of-concept than a fully validated contribution.

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper rigorously derives the locally optimal SMC proposal (Prop. 2), proves uniqueness of the minimum-variance proposal (Cor. 1), and derives a tractable surrogate log-variance objective with an upper-bound guarantee (Prop. 3), all with complete proofs in the appendix.

Extends the discrete-time importance weight derivation to a continuous-time (CTMC) formulation (Prop. 1) and explicitly connects/reconciles the result with existing continuous-time SMC works (Holderrieth et al. 2025; Lee et al. 2025), situating the contribution well within the literature.

Broad and fairly large-scale empirical validation spanning four distinct domains: 2D/MNIST synthetic tasks, toxic-text language modeling with MDLM, DNA regulatory sequence design, and text-to-image generation (MaskGit/ImageNet256 and Meissonic at scale with LoRA finetuning across 8 GPUs) — a good breadth for a single paper.

Careful attention to practical implementation details, e.g., deriving how to compute importance weights under the practically important but non-trivial low-confidence sampling scheme (Appendix C.2), and swapping in ReMDM sampling to preserve tractability for the CFG/MaskGit experiments.
Reasonably thorough ablations (λt schedule, number of Monte Carlo samples M) and reward-convergence plots that lend credibility to the amortized proposal training procedure.
Consistent and fairly large empirical gains from SMC over baselines (BoN, pretrained, non-SMC proposals) across metrics, and clear demonstration of scaling behavior with particle count N.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly names Singhal et al. (2025) and Dang et al. (2025) as the most closely related prior works, but no direct empirical head-to-head comparison against these baselines is provided in the main results — the comparisons instead focus on internal ablations (SMCbase/grad/amot vs BoN/pretrained), weakening the claim of clear superiority over prior SMC-for-discrete-diffusion methods.

The importance weight for the product-target (CFG) case (Eq. 6) relies on a detailed-balance approximation that is acknowledged to introduce approximation error whenever the reverse model is imperfect, but this error is never quantified or empirically bounded.

SMCamot exhibits a notable loss of diversity/quality in several settings (e.g., Dist-1/2/3 drops substantially in Table 1, and reduced sample diversity noted in the MoG/MNIST synthetic experiments), which is in some tension with the paper's stated motivation of avoiding the reward over-optimization pathology of fine-tuning methods — since the amortized proposal itself is a trained/finetuned component.

Wall-clock/compute overhead of the proposed methods (training the amortized proposal network and Fψ, additional forward passes for first-order gradient approximation) is not clearly reported or compared against baseline runtime, making it hard to assess practical cost-benefit tradeoffs, especially versus simple fine-tuning or guidance baselines.

Several main results tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 2, image-generation tables) report single-run numbers without variance/confidence intervals, unlike the DNA design experiment which does report std across seeds — this limits confidence in the significance of reported gains, particularly for close comparisons (e.g., SMCgrad vs SMCamot in some metrics).

The manuscript is dense with heavy notation and many propositions/derivations pushed to a very long appendix; while thorough, this reduces the self-contained clarity of the main text and could be streamlined for readability.

strengths: Proposes a principled SMC framework for discrete diffusion models with explicit derivation of tractable importance weights for both product (CFG-style) and reward-tilting targets, along with a careful characterization of the locally optimal proposal (Proposition 2) and its approximations.

Two concrete and reasonably well-motivated approximations to the optimal proposal are introduced: a first-order Taylor/gradient-based proposal and an amortized proposal trained via a log-variance (upper-bound) objective with a learned control variate, supported by a uniqueness proof (Corollary 1, Proposition 3).

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning synthetic 2D/MNIST tasks, toxic language generation, DNA sequence design, and large-scale text-to-image generation (MaskGit/ImageNet and Meissonic), showing consistent trends that more particles and better proposals improve reward alignment.

Extension to continuous-time CTMC diffusion (Proposition 1) connects the discrete-time derivation to existing continuous-time SMC/guidance literature (Holderrieth et al., Lee et al.), providing a unifying perspective.

Practical engineering details are provided (handling low-confidence/ReMDM sampling, twisted intermediate targets, Gumbel-softmax reparameterization for non-differentiable clean-data rewards), which aids reproducibility and real-world applicability to state-of-the-art samplers.
weaknesses: The core theoretical novelty is limited: the locally-optimal-proposal result (Proposition 2) is a well-known classical fact from the auxiliary particle filter / SMC literature, merely re-derived in the discrete diffusion setting; the continuous-time result explicitly "coincides" with Holderrieth et al. and Lee et al., further narrowing the claimed contribution to the amortized proposal and its log-variance training objective.

The importance weight for the product-target (CFG) case relies on a detailed-balance approximation (pθ(xt-1)/pθ(xt) ≈ pθ(xt-1|xt)/p(xt|xt-1)) that is only valid for a perfectly trained model; no theoretical bound or empirical quantification of this approximation error is given, undermining the claim of "tractable" and principled weights for this setting.

A central motivating claim is that SMC avoids the reward over-optimization seen in fine-tuning methods, yet the amortized proposal (SMCamot) itself requires reward-specific fine-tuning and empirically exhibits clear diversity collapse (e.g., Dist-1/2/3 drops substantially in Table 1, reduced diversity in MoG/MNIST toy tasks), which is the same failure mode the paper claims to mitigate — this tension is acknowledged but not resolved or deeply analyzed.

Despite being described as "most closely related" to Singhal et al. (2025) and Dang et al. (2025), the paper does not provide a direct, clearly-labeled empirical comparison against these concurrent SMC-for-discrete-diffusion baselines beyond treating pretrained-proposal SMC (SMCbase) as a stand-in; this leaves the central claimed insight ("better proposals beat fixed proposals") only partially validated against the true competing methods.

Baseline comparisons in several experiments are relatively shallow: e.g., the large-scale image generation experiments (Table 2, CFG improvement) only ablate particle count/sampling scheme without comparing to other training-free guidance or reward-alignment baselines from the literature (Li et al. 2024, Nisonoff et al. 2024, Guo et al. 2024, etc.) that are discussed in related work but not benchmarked empirically.

The amortized proposal and first-order proposal both require access to differentiable rewards and additional per-task training (for Propamot) or costly gradient/Jacobian computation (for Propgrad), which somewhat erodes the inference-time/test-time-only framing emphasized in the introduction and title.

Some presentation issues remain (e.g., inconsistent subscripts in Eq. 6, minor typos, dense appendix proofs), and the paper would benefit from clearer discussion of computational overhead/wall-clock cost of SMC with N particles versus baselines, which is central to practical adoption of "test-time scaling."

strengths: Provides a principled and mathematically rigorous SMC framework for discrete diffusion models, with clean derivations of tractable importance weights for both product (CFG-like) and reward-tilting targets, plus proofs establishing the locally optimal proposal and the log-variance training objective (including uniqueness results via Corollary 1 and Proposition 3).

Proposes two practical and well-motivated approximations to the intractable optimal proposal: a first-order Taylor/gradient-based proposal (Propgrad) and a learnable amortised proposal (Propamot) trained via a stable, variance-reduced log-variance objective, addressing a genuine gap in prior SMC-for-diffusion works that treat the pretrained model as a fixed proposal.

Extends the discrete-time formulation to continuous-time CTMC diffusion (Proposition 1) and explicitly connects/derives relationships to concurrent works (Holderrieth et al. 2025; Lee et al. 2025), showing good scholarly grounding and technical depth.

Broad and convincing empirical validation across four very different domains (2D/MNIST synthetic tasks, toxic-text language modelling, DNA sequence design, and large-scale text-to-image generation with MaskGit/Meissonic), consistently showing that better proposals (SMCamot > SMCgrad > SMCbase) improve reward alignment and that performance scales with particle count.

Careful practical engineering: addresses subtleties like computing importance weights under low-confidence sampling (a nontrivial technical contribution in Appendix C.2), and swaps in ReMDM sampling to preserve tractability, with supporting ablations validating this choice.

Thorough ablation studies (λt schedule, number of Monte Carlo samples M, sampling scheme comparisons) and extensive appendix material (proofs, hyperparameters, qualitative samples) that support reproducibility and give confidence in the robustness of the claims.
weaknesses: The importance weight for the product-distribution (CFG) case relies on a detailed-balance approximation that is only exact for a perfectly trained model, introducing a source of bias not fully quantified empirically (e.g., no direct ablation isolating this approximation error).

SMCamot, while achieving the best reward alignment, frequently sacrifices diversity/sample quality (e.g., large drop in Dist-1/2/3 and higher PPL in toxic-text generation, mode-seeking behavior in DNA design), suggesting a reward-over-optimization risk similar to the fine-tuning baselines the paper aims to avoid; this trade-off deserves more explicit discussion/quantification.

The gradient-based proposal (Propgrad) requires differentiable, cheaply-evaluable rewards and treats discrete rewards as continuous via a Taylor expansion, which is a heuristic with unclear error bounds in high dimensions/large vocabularies.

The amortised proposal must be retrained per task/reward, which somewhat undercuts the practical inference-time flexibility that guidance-based/training-free methods are supposed to offer, and training costs/compute are not compared against fine-tuning baselines (e.g., RL-based methods) in terms of wall-clock or sample efficiency.

Comparisons to alternative alignment approaches are somewhat limited in the main text (e.g., RL-based fine-tuning methods mentioned as motivation in the introduction are not empirically benchmarked against to substantiate the over-optimization claim), and direct comparisons with the most closely related concurrent SMC works (Singhal et al. 2025; Dang et al. 2025) are only discussed qualitatively rather than empirically.
The continuous-time SMC extension (Proposition 1, Appendix B) is purely theoretical with no corresponding experiments, leaving its practical utility unverified.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., garbled/typo'd equations such as 'Multinormial', 'desnoising', inconsistent notation for the forward kernel across sections) slightly hinder readability, though they do not undermine the technical content.
